content: Endometritis is a condition that can be classified histopathologically into two subtypes: acute endometritis and chronic endometritis (CE). Acute endometritis typically occurs following events such as abortion, childbirth, menstruation, uterine curettage, or intrauterine device (IUD) insertion. Symptoms of acute endometritis may include fever, pelvic pain, and vaginal discharge. Histologically, acute endometritis is characterized by the presence of numerous neutrophils in the endometrial stroma. Chronic endometritis, on the other hand, is often asymptomatic or associated with vague symptoms. It is a potential cause of infertility. Histologically, chronic endometritis is identified by the presence of plasma cells in the endometrial stroma. Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause a subtype of chronic endometritis known as chronic granulomatous endometritis, particularly in some developing countries. Pyometra is a rare disorder characterized by the accumulation of pus in the uterine cavity due to abnormal uterine drainage. It is most commonly seen in postmenopausal women and is associated with conditions such as atrophic cervicitis due to aging, IUD use, gynecologic tumors (malignant or benign), and radiation cervicitis. The classic triad of symptoms in pyometra includes lower abdominal pain, purulent vaginal discharge, and postmenopausal bleeding. Postpartum endometritis is caused by the ascent of bacteria, typically vaginal microflora, from the lower genital tract during labor. These bacteria colonize the cervix, ascend into the lower uterus, and may enter the amniotic fluid. The weakening and rupture of amniotic membranes, often due to collagenases and proteases, facilitate this process. In some cases, bacterial colonization of the decidua and amniotic fluid occurs without membrane rupture. Deciduitis may lead to myometrial infection, which can progress to postpartum endometritis if untreated, though antibiotic therapy after delivery often prevents this progression. In chronic endometritis, B-cells, which are normally confined to the basal layer of the endometrium, are found in both the functional and basal layers. These B-cells invade the glandular lumina and are associated with increased levels of IL-6, a differentiation factor for mature B-cells, and TNF-α, which enhances estrogen biosynthesis in endometrial glandular cells. Chronic endometritis may also involve abnormal expression of adhesion molecules and chemokines, such as CD62E, CXCL1, and CXCL13, which facilitate B-cell extravasation and migration. This condition is associated with endometrial micropolyposis, as seen on hysteroscopy, and may negatively impact embryo implantation. The prevalence of chronic endometritis is approximately 10–11% in biopsies from hysterectomies performed for gynecologic conditions. It is more common in infertile women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) and in those with recurrent implantation failure (RIF) or recurrent pregnancy losses (RPL). Studies have reported a prevalence of 15% in infertile women with IVF, 42% in women with RIF, and 8% in women with three or more RPLs. The diagnosis of acute endometritis is based on histological findings, including a large number of neutrophils in the endometrial stroma. Chronic endometritis is diagnosed via endometrial biopsy, with the presence of plasma cells in the stroma serving as the histological criterion. Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for CD138, a plasma cell-specific antigen, has higher sensitivity for diagnosing chronic endometritis compared to hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Imaging studies, such as ultrasound and CT scans, are not typically helpful in diagnosing endometritis but may be used to rule out other conditions in postpartum patients unresponsive to therapy. Fluid hysteroscopy can aid in diagnosing chronic endometritis by identifying findings such as stromal edema, micropolyps, and focal or diffuse hyperemia. Treatment of endometritis generally involves antibiotics. Surgical intervention may be necessary if there is a drainable fluid collection due to infection. Preventive measures for puerperal genital tract infections include routine antepartum screening and treatment of group B Streptococcus (GBS) and other infections, handwashing, aseptic procedures, and limiting invasive procedures. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the World Health Organization (WHO) recommend antimicrobial prophylaxis 60 minutes prior to cesarean delivery to reduce the risk of uterine and wound infections.
